items.title: Left and right cosets $gH$ and $Hg$ of a subgroup
items.strategy: No well-definedness obligation: $gH := \{gh : h \in H\}$ is an image of a set under a map, so it exists by replacement/separation as every other image in the library does. State BOTH sides ($gH$ and $Hg$) here, because the whole page turns on their difference; and state that $eH = H$ and that $g \in gH$, both immediate, since every later item uses them.

items.title: The relation $a \sim_H b \iff a^{-1}b \in H$ is an equivalence relation on $G$ whose class of $a$ is $aH$; hence the left cosets partition $G$, and $aH = bH$ if and only if $a^{-1}b \in H$
For every $g \in G$ the map $h \mapsto gh$ is a bijection $H \to gH$, so every left coset is equinumerous with $H$; likewise $h \mapsto hg$ is a bijection $H \to Hg$
The map $gH \mapsto Hg^{-1}$ is a well-defined bijection from the set of left cosets of $H$ onto the set of right cosets, so the two sets are equinumerous
A subset of a finite set is finite, a surjective image of a finite set is finite, and if $A \approx n$ and $B \subseteq A$ with $B \approx m$ then $m \le n$, with equality only when $B = A$

If $A \approx n$, $B \approx m$ and $A \cap B = \varnothing$ then $A \cup B \approx n + m$; and if $P$ is a set of pairwise disjoint sets with $P \approx k$, each member equinumerous with a fixed set of $m$ elements, then $\bigcup P \approx k \cdot m$
Divisibility in $\mathbb{N}$, prime and composite natural numbers
items.strategy: Two obligations. (1) DICTIONARY, not a second notion: $d \mid n$ is defined here for $d, n \in \mathbb{N}$ by $\exists q \in \mathbb{N},\, n = dq$, and the definition item must PROVE, not assert, that for naturals this agrees with the integer relation $\iota(d) \mid \iota(n)$ already defined in the published `thm-division-algorithm-in-z` (use that $\iota$ of `lem-nat-embeds-int` is injective, multiplicative, order-preserving, with image exactly the nonnegative integers; treat $d = 0$ separately, where both relations say $n = 0$). Silent re-definition is the level-7 two-notions-of-open defect. (2) INDEX/BOUNDARY: fix $p$ prime to mean $p \ge 2$ and the only $d \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d \mid p$ are $1$ and $p$; state explicitly that $0$ and $1$ are neither prime nor composite, and that $d \mid 0$ for every $d$ while $0 \mid n$ only for $n = 0$.

items.title: The set $G/H$ of left cosets and the index $[G:H]$
items.strategy: Three obligations, all discharged by items proved above and none to be waved through. (1) $G/H$ is a legitimate set of classes because it is the quotient set of the equivalence relation of `lem-coset-partition`, so cite `def-equivalence-relation` for the quotient-set construction rather than building a new one. (2) $[G:H] := |G/H|$ names a UNIQUE natural number only because a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural: cite claim 3 of `lem-pigeonhole`, exactly as the published `def-order-in-a-group` does for $|G|$. (3) THE DEFINITE ARTICLE: 'the index' presupposes that counting left cosets and counting right cosets give the same answer; that is `lem-left-and-right-cosets-equinumerous`, which must be proved first and cited here. Finiteness of $G$ is NOT assumed: the index is defined for any $G$ and $H$, and is written $\infty$ when $G/H$ is not finite, with $\infty$ a reserved symbol and no arithmetic performed on it (follow `def-order-in-a-group`).

items.title: Lagrange's theorem: if $G$ is a finite group and $H \le G$ then $H$ and $G/H$ are finite and $|G| = [G:H] \cdot |H|$; in particular $|H|$ divides $|G|$
In a finite group the order of every element divides the order of the group
$g^{|G|} = e$ for every element $g$ of a finite group $G$
A group whose order is a prime number is cyclic, is generated by any one of its non-identity elements, and has no subgroups other than $\{e\}$ and itself
For subgroups $K \le H \le G$ of a finite group, $[G:K] = [G:H]\,[H:K]$
What $g^{|G|} = e$ becomes in $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^{\times}$, and what a proof of that instance still requires
items.strategy: A `rem-` item, so it STATES and does not establish; every sentence in it is nevertheless held to the Statement standard. It records that Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem are the single group-theoretic fact `cor-g-to-the-group-order-is-identity` read in the group of units of $\mathbb{Z}/n$, and that what is still missing at this point is not group theory but the ring $\mathbb{Z}/n$ together with the characterisation of its units as the classes of integers coprime to $n$, which rests on Bezout's identity. PHRASE EVERY CLAIM AS A CLAIM ABOUT WHAT A PROOF REQUIRES, never about what the library contains: 'a proof of that instance requires Bezout's identity' never decays, 'this library has no number theory' decays the moment order 38 is built. Name `euclidean-domains-pids-and-unique-factorisation` in PLAIN PROSE and do NOT wikilink it: it is a page id, not an item id, and its items are not yet planned, so a link would be a dangling forward reference.

title: Cosets and Lagrange's Theorem: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ the left cosets of $n\mathbb{Z} = \langle n \rangle$ in $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ are the $n$ congruence classes $a + n\mathbb{Z}$, so $[\mathbb{Z} : n\mathbb{Z}] = n$, while $[\mathbb{Z} : \{0\}]$ is infinite
For any group $G$, $[G : G] = 1$ and $[G : \{e\}] = |G|$, so Lagrange's identity reads $|G| = 1 \cdot |G|$ and $|G| = |G| \cdot 1$ at the two ends

The subgroups of $\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,2,3\})$ are the trivial one, three of order $2$ generated by the transpositions, one of order $3$ generated by a $3$-cycle, and the whole group; every one of the orders $1, 2, 3, 6$ divides $6$
A left coset that is not a right coset: for $H = \{\mathrm{id}, (1\,2)\}$ and $g = (1\,3)$ in $\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,2,3\})$, $gH = \{(1\,3), (1\,2\,3)\}$ and $Hg = \{(1\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}$
In a cyclic group of order $n$, every divisor $d$ of $n$ is the order of a subgroup: if $n = dc$ then $\langle g^{c} \rangle$ has order $d$
Lagrange has no equinumerosity analogue for infinite groups: $2\mathbb{Z}$ has index $2$ in $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ and is equinumerous with $\mathbb{Z}$

The set $HK = \{hk\}$ of products of two subgroups need not be a subgroup: in $\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,2,3\})$, $H = \{\mathrm{id},(1\,2)\}$ and $K = \{\mathrm{id},(1\,3)\}$ give a four-element $HK$, and $4$ does not divide $6$
Every left coset of a subgroup is itself a subgroup

title: Rings, Subrings, Integral Domains and Fields

items.title: Ring: an abelian group under addition and a monoid under multiplication, with multiplication distributing over addition on both sides
items.strategy: CONVENTION DECISION, to be stated in the item and never silently assumed: a ring HAS a multiplicative identity, because $(R,\cdot,1)$ is required to be a monoid (`def-semigroup-and-monoid`). This is the Wikipedia and modern convention, and it is forced anyway by the scaffold's own wording. A structure satisfying every axiom except the existence of $1$ is a NON-UNITAL RING, is named as such, and is NOT called a ring here; `cex-2z-is-not-a-subring` on the companion page is the witness that the distinction has content. Well-definedness: 'the' zero and 'the' identity are legitimate only through the published `lem-identity-unique`, and 'the' additive inverse $-a$ only through `lem-inverse-unique`; cite both rather than assert uniqueness, exactly as `def-group` does. Distributivity must be stated on BOTH sides, since multiplication is not assumed commutative here and the published `def-field` states only the left form.

items.title: Commutative ring
In any ring $0 \cdot a = a \cdot 0 = 0$, $(-a)b = a(-b) = -(ab)$, $(-a)(-b) = ab$, $(-1)a = -a$ and $a(b - c) = ab - ac$
Integer multiples in a ring: $(m + n)a = ma + na$, $m(a + b) = ma + mb$, $(ma)b = m(ab) = a(mb)$ and $(ma)(nb) = (mn)(ab)$ for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $a, b \in R$
The units of a ring are the invertible elements of its multiplicative monoid, and $R^{\times}$ is a group under multiplication; $0 \in R^{\times}$ only in the zero ring
Zero divisor, and integral domain: a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$ and no zero divisors
items.strategy:
Boundary obligation, and a place a false Statement is easy to write: fix ONE convention for 'zero divisor' and keep it. Here $a$ is a zero divisor when $a 
e 0$ and $ab = 0$ for some $b 
e 0$; under that convention $0$ is not a zero divisor and the zero ring is excluded from being a domain by $1 
e 0$, not by the zero-divisor clause. State that $1 
e 0$ is a hypothesis and not a consequence.

items.title: Cancellation characterises domains: in a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$, $ab = ac$ with $a \ne 0$ forces $b = c$ if and only if the ring has no zero divisors
Division ring: a ring with $1 \ne 0$ in which every nonzero element is a unit
Every field is a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$; it is an integral domain, and it is a commutative division ring
Every commutative division ring is a field, so 'field' and 'commutative division ring' name the same structures and the published definition and the ring-theoretic one agree
Ordered ring: a ring with a total order compatible with addition and with positives closed under multiplication

The order presentation and the positive-cone presentation of an ordered ring determine each other: $P = \{x : 0 < x\}$ satisfies trichotomy and closure, and $a < b :\iff b - a \in P$ recovers the order
Every ordered field is an ordered ring, and its order is the one its positive cone induces
Subring: a subset containing $1_R$, closed under addition, additive inverses and multiplication
items.strategy: Well-definedness: the item must state and justify that the restricted operations really are binary operations on $S$ and that $(S,+,\cdot,0,1_R)$ is then a ring in its own right, with the SAME zero and the SAME identity as $R$ (the published `def-subgroup` and `lem-subgroup-criterion` do exactly this job for the additive part and must be cited rather than re-proved). Requiring $1_R \in S$ is forced by the convention fixed in `def-ring`; say so, and point at `cex-2z-is-not-a-subring`.

items.title: Subring criterion: $S \subseteq R$ is a subring if and only if $1_R \in S$ and $a - b \in S$ and $ab \in S$ for all $a, b \in S$; and an intersection of subrings is a subring
Subfield: a subring of a field that is closed under inverses of its nonzero elements, and is therefore a field with the restricted operations
items.strategy: Well-definedness: 'is therefore a field' is a claim and must be discharged inside the item, by checking the axioms of the published `def-field` for the restricted operations, using `lem-commutative-division-ring-is-a-field` rather than re-deriving. Also state that $0_K = 0_F$ and $1_K = 1_F$, which is what makes a subfield of an ordered field inherit the order, and which the vector-space page (order 60) relies on when it restricts scalars.

items.title: Ring homomorphism: additive, multiplicative, and required to send $1$ to $1$
items.strategy: The requirement $f(1_R) = 1_S$ must be IMPOSED, not derived: the situation is exactly the published `def-group-homomorphism`, where preservation of the identity is free for groups and must be assumed for monoids. Say which of the two is happening here (the multiplicative part is only a monoid) and point at `cex-ring-homomorphism-not-preserving-identity` on the companion page as the witness that the clause is not redundant.

items.title: A ring homomorphism satisfies $f(0) = 0$, $f(-a) = -f(a)$ and $f(ma) = m f(a)$ for $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, carries units to units, and has a subring as its image; composites of ring homomorphisms are ring homomorphisms
A ring homomorphism between fields is a field homomorphism in the published sense, and every such map is injective
The product ring $R \times S$ with componentwise operations, its identity $(1_R, 1_S)$ and its units $R^{\times} \times S^{\times}$
items.strategy: Well-definedness is cheap here but must still be written: the componentwise rules really are binary operations on $R \times S$ and the axioms hold componentwise. State the two facts that later items use: the product of two rings with $1 \ne 0$ is never a domain, because $(1,0)(0,1) = (0,0)$; and the product is commutative exactly when both factors are.

items.title: The ring $R^{X}$ of all functions from a set $X$ into a ring, with pointwise operations
items.strategy: Well-definedness: the pointwise rules are binary operations on $R^{X}$ and every axiom is checked pointwise; the zero and the identity are the constant functions. This item is also the ANCHOR the vector-space page (order 60) points back to: the SAME set $F^{X}$ carries a vector-space structure there, with the SAME addition and a different second operation, and page 60 links here rather than re-deriving the additive structure. State that $R^{X}$ has zero divisors as soon as $X$ has two elements and $R \ne 0$, and that $R^{X}$ is commutative exactly when $R$ is.

items.title: The characteristic of a ring: the least $n \ge 1$ with $n \cdot 1_R = 0$ when one exists, and $0$ otherwise
items.strategy: Two obligations. (1) EXISTENCE OF THE LEAST: the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : n \ge 1,\ n \cdot 1_R = 0\}$ has a least element when nonempty, by `thm-well-ordering-principle`; this is the same shape as the published `def-order-in-a-group` and should be written the same way, with $0$ (not $\infty$) as the value in the empty case, which is the standard convention. (2) DICTIONARY, not a second notion: $n \cdot 1_R$ here is the additive power of the published `def-group-power` applied to the additive group of $R$, and for a FIELD it is exactly the map $\iota$ of the published `def-canonical-natural`. Prove the agreement (both satisfy the same recursion $\iota(0) = 0$, $\iota(\sigma(n)) = \iota(n) + 1$, and `thm-recursion` gives uniqueness) rather than asserting it, and note that a natural number is a von Neumann natural and so is not itself an element of $R$.

items.title: The characteristic of an integral domain is $0$ or a prime number

title: Rings, Domains and Fields: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\mathbb{Z}$ is a commutative ring with identity and an ordered ring, the published construction being an instance of the general definitions
$\mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain whose group of units is $\{1,-1\}$, so it is not a field: $2$ is nonzero and not invertible
$\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are fields, hence commutative rings, integral domains and ordered rings
The Cauchy sequences of rationals form a commutative ring that is a subring of $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and is not an integral domain
The quaternions $\mathbb{H}$: a division ring that is not a field, with $q^{-1} = \bar q / N(q)$ for $q \ne 0$
A product of two nonzero rings always has zero divisors: $(1,0)(0,1) = (0,0)$ in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$, so a product of integral domains is never an integral domain
$2\mathbb{Z}$ is closed under addition, negation and multiplication and is not a subring of $\mathbb{Z}$, because it does not contain $1$
The zero ring $\{0\}$, in which $1 = 0$: a commutative ring that is not a domain, not a division ring and not a field, of characteristic $1$
The map $n \mapsto (n,0)$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ preserves addition and multiplication and does not preserve $1$, so the clause $f(1) = 1$ is not redundant
In every commutative ring, each nonzero element is either a unit or a zero divisor

title: Vector Spaces, Subspaces, Span and Direct Sums

items.title: Vector space over a field: an abelian group together with a scalar multiplication satisfying the four compatibility axioms
items.strategy: Three things this item must get right. (1) THE FIELD IS THE PUBLISHED ONE: cite `def-field` (order 9) and do not restate the field axioms. (2) THE ADDITIVE PART IS AN ABELIAN GROUP, in the published sense of `def-group`: say so explicitly, so that associativity, commutativity, the uniqueness of $0_V$ (`lem-identity-unique`) and the uniqueness of $-v$ (`lem-inverse-unique`) are inherited and are never re-derived here. (3) SCALAR MULTIPLICATION IS NOT A BINARY OPERATION ON A SET: it is a map $F \times V \to V$, so `def-binary-operation` does not apply to it and must not be cited for it. State the four axioms as $\lambda(u+v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$, $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$, $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$, $1_F v = v$, and note that the last is an axiom and not a consequence.

items.title: In any vector space $0_F v = 0_V$, $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$, $(-\lambda)v = -(\lambda v)$, $(-1_F)v = -v$, and $\lambda v = 0_V$ forces $\lambda = 0_F$ or $v = 0_V$
The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$
items.strategy: Well-definedness: the pointwise rules are genuinely a map $F^{X} \times F^{X} \to F^{X}$ and a map $F \times F^{X} \to F^{X}$, and each axiom is checked pointwise from the field axioms. INDEX DISCIPLINE, and this is the single most likely defect on the page: a natural number here is a von Neumann natural, so $n = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ (`lem-nat-order-is-membership`) and the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, NOT $x_1, \dots, x_n$. Every displayed tuple on this page and its companion must start at index $0$. State the two boundary cases: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, so it is the zero space; and $F^{1}$ is $F$ up to the obvious identification. DICTIONARY: the same set $F^{X}$ carries the ring structure of `def-ring-of-functions` (order 34), with the SAME addition and with pointwise multiplication in place of scalar multiplication; link that item in `## Remarks` and say which operation is which, so the two structures are never conflated.

items.title: The vector space $M_{m \times n}(F) := F^{\,m \times n}$ of $m$ by $n$ matrices over a field, with entrywise operations
items.strategy: This item introduces ONLY the vector-space structure and the notation $a_{ij}$; the matrix product, the ring $M_n(F)$ and the matrix of a linear map belong to order 66 and must NOT be anticipated here, not even in a remark that would need them. Index discipline as in `def-function-space`: rows are indexed by $i \in m = \{0,\dots,m-1\}$ and columns by $j \in n$, both starting at $0$.

items.title: A field is a vector space over itself, and over any subfield $K \subseteq F$ every $F$-vector space is a $K$-vector space by restricting the scalars
Linear subspace of a vector space
items.strategy: NAMING, decided at step 1 and to be honoured: the id says LINEAR subspace and the title says it too, because the library already uses 'subspace' for the topological notion (`def-subspace-topology`, order 96) and the two are unrelated. Do not link the topological item and do not remark on it; the qualified name is the whole fix. Well-definedness: state that the restricted operations really are a vector addition and a scalar multiplication on $W$, and that $(W,+,0_V)$ is then a vector space whose zero and whose negatives are those of $V$ (that half is `lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup`, proved next, and is cited rather than re-argued).

items.title: The additive group of a vector space is an abelian group and every linear subspace is a subgroup of it; conversely a subgroup closed under scalar multiplication is a linear subspace
One-step subspace test: a nonempty $W \subseteq V$ is a linear subspace if and only if $\lambda u + v \in W$ for all $\lambda \in F$ and $u, v \in W$
The intersection of a nonempty family of linear subspaces of $V$ is a linear subspace of $V$
Linear combination of a finite list, and the span $\operatorname{span}(S)$ as the smallest linear subspace containing $S$
items.strategy: Well-definedness, in the shape the published `def-generated-subgroup` already uses and which must be reused rather than invented: the family of linear subspaces containing $S$ is nonempty because $V$ belongs to it, so its intersection is a linear subspace by `lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces`, and that intersection is the SMALLEST subspace containing $S$; those two properties determine it, which is what licenses the definite article. A linear combination is $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to V$, the sum being the finite product of the published `def-monoid-finite-product` read additively in the abelian group $(V,+)$: cite it, do NOT define a new finite sum, and note that `def-finite-sum` is unavailable because it is stated for sequences into the complete ordered field. Index from $0$, and state that the empty combination ($n = 0$) is $0_V$, so $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ as a consequence and not as a stipulation.

items.title: $\operatorname{span}(S)$ is exactly the set of linear combinations of finite lists of elements of $S$, and $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
The span is monotone and idempotent, $\operatorname{span}(S) = S$ exactly when $S$ is a linear subspace, and $\operatorname{span}(S \cup \{0_V\}) = \operatorname{span}(S)$
$\operatorname{span}\{v\} = \{\lambda v : \lambda \in F\}$, which is $\{0_V\}$ when $v = 0_V$ and otherwise meets $\{0_V\}$ only there
The sum $U + W$ of two linear subspaces and the sum $\sum_{i<n} U_i$ of a finite family
items.strategy: Well-definedness and boundary: the sum is defined as the set of all $\sum_{i<n} u_i$ with $u_i \in U_i$, the finite sum again being `def-monoid-finite-product` read additively; the item must prove that this set IS a linear subspace rather than assert it. Index from $0$, and state the empty case: the sum of the empty family ($n = 0$) is $\{0_V\}$, which is what makes the induction in `lem-sum-is-span-of-union` start.

items.title: $\sum_{i<n} U_i = \operatorname{span}\bigl(\bigcup_{i<n} U_i\bigr)$, so the sum is the smallest linear subspace containing every $U_i$
Internal direct sum $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$: the sum is everything and each summand meets the sum of the others only in $0_V$
items.strategy: THE TRAP THIS ITEM EXISTS TO AVOID: for three or more summands, PAIRWISE trivial intersections are NOT sufficient, and the condition must be stated as $U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$ for every $j < n$. Writing the pairwise condition would make the definition false, and the companion page carries `cex-pairwise-trivial-intersection-is-not-a-direct-sum` as the witness. State the two-summand case explicitly as the familiar $V = U + W$ with $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and say that for two summands the two conditions do coincide. Index from $0$; the empty direct sum ($n = 0$) is the zero space.

items.title: $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$ if and only if every $v \in V$ is $\sum_{i<n} u_i$ with $u_i \in U_i$ in exactly one way; equivalently, if and only if the sum is $V$ and $\sum_{i<n} u_i = 0_V$ with $u_i \in U_i$ forces every $u_i = 0_V$

title: Vector Spaces and Subspaces: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\mathbb{R}$ is a vector space over itself and, by restriction of scalars along the embedded copy of $\mathbb{Q}$, a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$
In $F^{3}$ the three coordinate lines are linear subspaces whose internal direct sum is $F^{3}$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space
$F^{\mathbb{N}}$ is a vector space and the eventually zero families form a linear subspace of it that is the span of the standard unit families
The first quadrant of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ contains $0$ and is closed under addition and is not a linear subspace, since it is not closed under multiplication by $-1$
The union of the two coordinate axes of $F^{2}$ is closed under scalar multiplication and is not closed under addition, so neither closure condition implies the other
Three lines in $F^{2}$ that meet pairwise only in $0$ and whose sum is $F^{2}$ with decompositions that are not unique, so pairwise trivial intersection does not give a direct sum
Two planes in $F^{3}$ whose sum is $F^{3}$ and whose intersection is a line, computed explicitly
The union of two linear subspaces is a linear subspace
